Complementary information — The retrieved documents provide varied examples and evidence of animals understanding human language, focusing on different species and aspects without contradiction.

The retrieved documents all agree that some animals can understand human language but provide complementary details: d1 focuses on dogs, apes, and dolphins with specific studies; d2 highlights dogs, pigs, chimps, elephants, parrots, and gorillas like Koko; d3 discusses nonverbal cues and linguistic abilities of parrots; d4 adds sea lions and elephants; d5 delves deeper into dogs' object-name mapping. Each document adds different species, examples, or facets of understanding (words, commands, nonverbal cues) without conflicting claims.

Together, these documents show that animals' understanding of human language is not uniform but varies across species and contexts, with multiple studies supporting the ability in specific animals. The evidence is complementary, illustrating different dimensions of the phenomenon.

Some animals can understand human language, as shown by studies on specific species. Dogs like Rico and Chaser can learn the names of hundreds of objects and respond to commands [d1][d5]. Other animals, such as bonobo ape Kanzi [d1], grey parrot Alex [d3], gorilla Koko [d2], and sea lion Rio [d4], also demonstrate comprehension of words or symbols. Understanding ranges from recognizing words and commands to interpreting nonverbal cues like tone and body language [d3]. The evidence collectively indicates that certain animals, especially those closely interacting with humans, can achieve significant linguistic understanding.
